stem: Approximately what proportion of the Earth's surface is covered by water (oceans)?
solution: Approximately 71% (about 70–71%) of the Earth's surface is covered by water — mainly the oceans — while only about 29% is land. Because of this vast expanse of water, the Earth is often called the 'Blue Planet' or 'Watery Planet'. The oceans are a single connected body of salt water, conventionally divided into the major oceans (Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern/Antarctic, and Arctic). Understanding that ~71% of the Earth is covered by water is a fundamental prelims point. About 71% of the Earth's surface is covered by water (oceans).

stem: The largest and deepest ocean in the world is the:
solution: The Pacific Ocean is the largest and deepest ocean in the world. It covers about one-third of the Earth's surface (more than all the land put together), and it contains the deepest known point on Earth — the Mariana Trench (with the Challenger Deep, about 11,000 m deep). The Pacific is roughly circular/triangular in shape and is bordered by the Ring of Fire (a zone of volcanoes and earthquakes). (The other oceans, in decreasing size, are the Atlantic, the Indian, the Southern, and the Arctic.) Understanding that the Pacific is the largest and deepest ocean is a prelims point. The Pacific is the largest and deepest ocean in the world.

stem: The deepest known point in the world's oceans, located in the Pacific Ocean, is the:
solution: The Mariana Trench, located in the western Pacific Ocean (near the Mariana Islands), contains the deepest known point in the world's oceans — a spot called the Challenger Deep, about 11,000 metres (roughly 11 km) below sea level. This is deeper than Mount Everest is tall. Ocean trenches like the Mariana are the deepest parts of the ocean floor, formed at subduction zones (where one plate dives beneath another). Understanding that the Mariana Trench is the deepest point on Earth is a prelims point. The Mariana Trench (Challenger Deep) in the Pacific is the deepest known point in the oceans.

stem: The study of the oceans (their features, water, life, and movements) is called:
solution: Oceanography is the scientific study of the oceans — including their physical features (the ocean floor, its relief), the properties of ocean water (temperature, salinity), the movements of ocean water (waves, tides, currents), and marine life. Oceanographers explore and study the vast, largely-hidden world of the oceans. (Compare: cartography is map-making, meteorology is the study of weather/atmosphere, seismology is the study of earthquakes.) Understanding the term oceanography is a prelims point. Oceanography is the study of the oceans.

stem: The relief of the ocean floor includes the gently-sloping, shallow submerged margin of the continents (rich in fisheries and where the sea is shallow) called the:
solution: The continental shelf is the gently-sloping, shallow, submerged extension (margin) of a continent — the shallow seabed bordering the land, extending from the shoreline out to the point where the slope becomes steeper (the shelf break). It is usually shallow (generally less than about 200 m deep) and covered by shallow seas. Continental shelves are very important: they are the richest fishing grounds in the world (sunlight reaches the shallow water, supporting plankton and fish), and they often hold deposits of petroleum and natural gas. Understanding the continental shelf (shallow submerged continental margin, rich fisheries) is a prelims point. The continental shelf is the shallow, gently-sloping submerged margin of a continent, rich in fisheries.

stem: Beyond the continental shelf, the ocean floor drops steeply. This steep slope leading down from the edge of the shelf to the deep ocean floor is called the:
solution: The continental slope is the steep slope that leads down from the outer edge of the continental shelf (the shelf break) to the deep ocean floor. It marks the boundary between the continents (the shallow, continental shelf) and the deep ocean basins. The continental slope is generally steep and is often cut by deep 'submarine canyons'. It lies at depths generally between about 200 m and 3000 m. Understanding the continental slope (the steep descent from shelf to deep sea) is a prelims point. The continental slope is the steep slope descending from the continental shelf to the deep ocean floor.

stem: The vast, flat, deep ocean floor (the largest part of the ocean floor, covering the deep-sea basins) is called the:
solution: The abyssal plain is the vast, flat, or gently-undulating deep ocean floor that covers the deep-sea basins — it is the largest part of the ocean floor. Abyssal plains lie at great depths (generally 3000–6000 m) and are among the flattest and smoothest regions on Earth, covered by fine sediments. They stretch across the deep ocean basins between the continental margins and the mid-oceanic ridges. Understanding the abyssal plain (the flat deep ocean floor) is a prelims point. The abyssal plain is the vast, flat deep-sea floor of the ocean basins.

stem: The long, underwater mountain ranges that run through the middle of the oceans (formed where new ocean crust is created at diverging plate boundaries) are called:
solution: Mid-oceanic ridges are the long, continuous, underwater mountain ranges (submarine mountain chains) that run through the middle of the oceans. They are formed at divergent (constructive) plate boundaries, where two plates move apart and molten rock (magma) rises up to create new ocean crust (sea-floor spreading). The mid-oceanic ridge system is the longest mountain chain on Earth, winding through all the ocean basins (for example, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge). Understanding mid-oceanic ridges (undersea mountain ranges at spreading boundaries) is a prelims point. Mid-oceanic ridges are underwater mountain ranges formed where plates diverge and new ocean crust is created.

stem: The deepest parts of the oceans — long, narrow, very deep depressions in the ocean floor (found near subduction zones, often bordering continents/island arcs) — are called:
solution: Ocean trenches (also called deeps) are the deepest parts of the oceans — long, narrow, steep-sided, very deep depressions or troughs in the ocean floor. They are typically found near the margins of oceans, often bordering continents or chains of volcanic islands (island arcs), and they mark subduction zones (where one tectonic plate dives down beneath another). The deepest ocean trench is the Mariana Trench in the Pacific. Trenches are associated with volcanic and earthquake activity. Understanding ocean trenches (the deepest ocean depressions at subduction zones) is a prelims point. Ocean trenches are the deepest, narrow depressions of the ocean floor, found at subduction zones.

stem: The correct order of the ocean-floor relief features, going from the coast outward to the deep sea, is:
options: Continental slope → continental shelf → abyssal plain
Continental shelf → continental slope → deep-sea (abyssal) plain
Abyssal plain → continental shelf → continental slope
Ocean trench → continental shelf → abyssal plain
solution: Going from the coast outward toward the deep sea, the major relief features of the ocean floor are, in order: (1) the continental shelf (the shallow, gently-sloping submerged margin of the continent, near the coast); (2) the continental slope (the steep slope descending from the edge of the shelf); and then (3) the deep-sea plain or abyssal plain (the vast, flat, deep ocean floor). (Beyond and within the abyssal plains lie other features like the mid-oceanic ridges and the deep ocean trenches.) So the sequence from land to deep ocean is: shelf → slope → abyssal plain. Understanding this order of ocean-floor features is a prelims point. From coast to deep sea, the order is: continental shelf → continental slope → abyssal (deep-sea) plain.

stem: The saltiness of ocean water — the amount of dissolved salts in it — is called:
solution: Salinity is the term for the saltiness of ocean water — that is, the total amount of dissolved salts present in a given quantity of sea water. It is usually expressed as the number of grams of dissolved salt in 1000 grams (1 kg) of sea water — that is, in 'parts per thousand' (‰ or ppt/psu). The average salinity of ocean water is about 35 parts per thousand (35‰), meaning about 35 grams of salt per kilogram of sea water. The most abundant salt in sea water is common salt (sodium chloride). Understanding salinity (the saltiness of sea water) is a prelims point. Salinity is the amount of dissolved salts in ocean water (average ~35 parts per thousand).

stem: The average salinity of the ocean water is about:
solution: The average salinity of the ocean water is about 35 parts per thousand (35‰) — that is, on average, about 35 grams of dissolved salts are present in every 1000 grams (1 kilogram) of sea water. Salinity varies from place to place: it is higher where evaporation is high and freshwater input is low (like enclosed subtropical seas), and lower where there is heavy rainfall or a large inflow of freshwater from rivers or melting ice (like near the equator, the poles, and river mouths). Understanding the average ocean salinity (~35‰) is a prelims point. The average salinity of ocean water is about 35 parts per thousand.

stem: Salinity of sea water is generally HIGHER where:
options: Rainfall is heavy and rivers add freshwater
Evaporation is high and there is little freshwater input (e.g., enclosed subtropical seas)
The water is very cold near the poles
solution: Salinity of sea water is generally higher where evaporation is high and there is little addition of freshwater. High evaporation (as in the hot subtropical and enclosed seas) removes water but leaves the salts behind, concentrating the salinity; and where few rivers, little rain, or little ice-melt add freshwater, there is nothing to dilute the salt. This is why enclosed subtropical seas with high evaporation and little freshwater inflow — like the Red Sea, the Mediterranean, and especially inland salt lakes like the Dead Sea and the Great Salt Lake — have very high salinity. Conversely, salinity is lower where rainfall is heavy, rivers add freshwater, or ice melts (like near the equator, at river mouths, and near the poles). Understanding what raises salinity (high evaporation, low freshwater input) is a prelims point. Salinity is higher where evaporation is high and freshwater input is low.

stem: One of the saltiest (highest-salinity) water bodies in the world, so salty that people float easily in it, is the:
solution: The Dead Sea (a salt lake between Israel and Jordan) is one of the saltiest water bodies in the world — with a salinity many times that of the ocean (around 240‰ or more, versus ~35‰ for the ocean). It is so salty because it lies in a hot, dry region with very high evaporation and no outlet (it is an enclosed inland lake, so salts brought in by rivers accumulate and become concentrated). Because the very salty water is so dense, objects (and people) float very easily on its surface. (The Great Salt Lake in the USA is another example of a very saline lake.) Understanding the Dead Sea as an example of extremely high salinity is a prelims point. The Dead Sea is one of the saltiest water bodies, so dense with salt that people float easily.

stem: The temperature of ocean-surface water generally __________ from the equator toward the poles.
solution: The temperature of ocean-surface water generally decreases from the equator toward the poles — that is, the surface water is warmest near the equator (where it receives the most insolation) and gets progressively colder toward the higher latitudes and the poles (which receive less insolation, and where ice-cold polar water occurs). This latitudinal pattern parallels the distribution of solar heating. (Ocean temperature also decreases with depth — the surface is warm, and deep water is cold everywhere.) Understanding that ocean-surface temperature decreases from equator to poles is a prelims point. Ocean-surface temperature decreases from the equator toward the poles.

stem: The temperature of ocean water generally __________ with increasing depth.
solution: The temperature of ocean water generally decreases with increasing depth. The surface layer of the ocean is warmed by the Sun and is therefore relatively warm (and it is mixed by winds and waves); but as one goes deeper, less and less of the Sun's heat penetrates, so the temperature falls. The decrease is most rapid in a middle layer called the 'thermocline' (where temperature drops quickly with depth), below which lies the cold, dark deep ocean, where the water is uniformly very cold (near freezing). So the ocean has warm surface water over cold deep water. Understanding that ocean temperature decreases with depth is a prelims point. Ocean-water temperature decreases with increasing depth.

stem: The layer in the ocean where temperature decreases rapidly with depth (separating the warm surface water from the cold deep water) is called the:
solution: The thermocline is the layer of the ocean, at intermediate depth, in which the water temperature decreases rapidly (sharply) with increasing depth — forming a transition zone that separates the warm, well-mixed surface layer above from the cold, deep water below. Above the thermocline, the surface water is relatively warm and of fairly uniform temperature (mixed by winds); within the thermocline, temperature drops quickly; and below it lies the cold deep ocean. The thermocline is an important feature of the ocean's vertical temperature structure. Understanding the thermocline (zone of rapid temperature decrease with depth) is a prelims point. The thermocline is the ocean layer where temperature falls rapidly with depth, between the warm surface and the cold deep water.

stem: The most abundant salt dissolved in sea water (the one that makes it taste salty) is:
solution: Sodium chloride (common salt, NaCl) is the most abundant salt dissolved in sea water — it makes up the largest share of the dissolved salts (roughly three-quarters of them) and is what gives sea water its characteristic salty taste. Sea water also contains many other dissolved salts and minerals (such as magnesium chloride, magnesium sulphate, calcium salts, potassium salts, etc.), but sodium chloride is by far the most plentiful. (This is why common salt can be obtained by evaporating sea water in salt pans.) Understanding that sodium chloride is the main salt in sea water is a prelims point. Sodium chloride (common salt) is the most abundant salt dissolved in sea water.

stem: Salinity is generally LOW near the mouths of large rivers and near the equator because:
options: Large amounts of freshwater are added (by rivers and by heavy equatorial rainfall), diluting the salt
There are no salts on Earth
solution: Salinity is generally low near the mouths of large rivers and near the equator because large amounts of freshwater are added there, diluting the salt. At river mouths, the rivers pour in huge quantities of freshwater, which mixes with and dilutes the sea water (lowering its salinity). Near the equator, the heavy convectional rainfall adds a lot of freshwater to the ocean surface (and the high humidity reduces net evaporation), again diluting the salt and lowering the salinity. So wherever plentiful freshwater is added (river inflow, heavy rain, or ice-melt near the poles), salinity is reduced. Understanding why salinity is low at river mouths and the equator (freshwater dilution) is a prelims point. Salinity is low near river mouths and the equator because added freshwater dilutes the salt.

stem: The continental shelf is very important economically mainly because it:
options: Is the deepest part of the ocean
Contains the richest fishing grounds and deposits of oil and natural gas
solution: The continental shelf is very important economically because it contains the richest fishing grounds in the world and important deposits of mineral resources — especially petroleum (oil) and natural gas. The shallow waters over the shelf allow sunlight to penetrate to the sea floor, supporting the growth of plankton (the base of the food chain), which makes these areas teem with fish — so most of the world's major fisheries are on the continental shelves. In addition, the sediments of many continental shelves hold valuable reserves of oil and natural gas (extracted by offshore drilling), and other minerals. Understanding the economic importance of the continental shelf (fisheries + oil/gas) is a prelims point. The continental shelf is economically important for its rich fisheries and its oil and natural gas deposits.

stem: The oceans are important for life on Earth because they:
options: Are a source of food (fish), minerals, and energy; a means of transport; and they regulate the climate and the water cycle
solution: The oceans are vitally important for life on Earth in many ways: they are a rich source of food (fish and other seafood), minerals (salt, and metals and minerals from the sea and sea floor), and energy (oil and natural gas from the shelf, and tidal/wave energy); they are the world's great highways of transport and trade (ships carry most of the world's goods across the oceans); they regulate the Earth's climate (by storing and redistributing heat through ocean currents, and by moderating temperatures); they drive the water cycle (most evaporation, and hence rainfall, comes from the oceans); and they produce much of the world's oxygen (through marine plants/phytoplankton) and support enormous biodiversity. Understanding the importance of the oceans is a prelims-relevant point. The oceans provide food, minerals, energy, and transport, and they regulate climate and the water cycle.

stem: Coral reefs (like the Great Barrier Reef) are built by tiny marine animals and grow best in:
options: Warm, shallow, clear, sunlit tropical waters
solution: Coral reefs are built by tiny marine animals (coral polyps), whose limestone (calcium carbonate) skeletons accumulate over time to form the reefs. Corals grow best in warm, shallow, clear, sunlit tropical and subtropical waters — they need warm water (roughly above 20°C), shallow depths and clear water (so that sunlight can reach the algae that live in partnership with the corals and provide them energy), and clean (unpolluted, sediment-free) water. This is why coral reefs are found in the tropics (like the Great Barrier Reef off Australia, the world's largest coral reef). Coral reefs are among the richest, most biodiverse ecosystems on Earth. (They are threatened by warming seas and ocean acidification — 'coral bleaching'.) Understanding the conditions for coral growth (warm, shallow, clear tropical seas) is a prelims point. Coral reefs grow best in warm, shallow, clear, sunlit tropical waters.

stem: The second-largest ocean in the world, roughly 'S'-shaped and lying between the Americas and Europe/Africa, is the:
solution: The Atlantic Ocean is the second-largest ocean in the world (after the Pacific). It has a characteristic 'S' shape and lies between the Americas (to the west) and Europe and Africa (to the east). It is bordered by highly indented coastlines with many bays and seas, and it contains the Mid-Atlantic Ridge running down its middle. Because it links the two great economic regions of North America/Europe, the Atlantic is the world's busiest ocean for trade. Understanding that the Atlantic is the second-largest ocean is a prelims point. The Atlantic is the second-largest ocean, S-shaped, between the Americas and Europe/Africa.

stem: The only ocean named after a country, bordered by Asia to the north (and by Africa and Australia), is the:
solution: The Indian Ocean is the only ocean named after a country — India. It is the third-largest ocean, bounded by Asia (including India) to the north, Africa to the west, Australia to the east, and the Southern Ocean/Antarctica to the south. Because it is landlocked to the north by the Asian landmass, its northern part experiences the seasonal reversal of the monsoon winds and currents. India occupies a central, strategic position in the Indian Ocean, which is important for India's trade and security. Understanding that the Indian Ocean is named after India is a prelims point. The Indian Ocean is the only ocean named after a country (India).

stem: Assertion (A): The continental shelves have the world's richest fishing grounds. Reason (R): The shallow water of the shelves allows sunlight to reach the sea floor, supporting the plankton on which fish feed. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the continental shelves have the world's richest fishing grounds. And the reason is (R) that the water over the shelves is shallow, so sunlight can penetrate to (or near) the sea floor; this sunlight supports the growth of tiny floating plants and organisms — plankton — which form the base of the marine food chain and provide abundant food for fish. The plentiful plankton (thanks to the shallow, sunlit water) is exactly why fish gather in such numbers over the shelves — so R correctly explains A. Understanding this cause-effect (shallow sunlit shelf → plankton → rich fisheries) is a prelims point. Continental shelves are rich fishing grounds because their shallow, sunlit water supports the plankton that fish feed on.

stem: An isolated, submerged (underwater) mountain or hill rising from the ocean floor (which does not reach the surface) is called a:
solution: A seamount is an isolated mountain (usually of volcanic origin) that rises from the ocean floor but does not reach the water's surface (its peak stays submerged). Seamounts have pointed tops and steep sides. (A related feature, a seamount with a flat, eroded top, is called a 'guyot'.) Seamounts are features of the deep ocean floor. Understanding the seamount (a submerged underwater mountain) is a prelims point. A seamount is an isolated submerged mountain rising from the ocean floor.

stem: A flat-topped submerged seamount (a former volcanic island whose top was eroded flat and then submerged) is called a:
solution: A guyot is a flat-topped seamount — a submerged, isolated undersea mountain (of volcanic origin) whose top is flat, having been eroded/planed off (typically by wave action when it once stood at or near the surface as an island) before it sank/submerged below the sea. Guyots are distinguished from ordinary seamounts (which have pointed tops) by their characteristic flat tops. They are features of the deep ocean floor. Understanding the guyot (flat-topped submerged seamount) is a prelims point. A guyot is a flat-topped submerged seamount.

stem: A ring-shaped coral reef (often enclosing a shallow lagoon), typically formed around a submerged or former volcanic island, is called an:
solution: An atoll is a ring-shaped (roughly circular or horseshoe-shaped) coral reef that encloses a shallow central lagoon. Atolls typically form around a former volcanic island: coral grows as a fringing reef around the island, and as the island slowly subsides (sinks), the coral keeps growing upward, eventually leaving a ring of reef (and low coral islands) surrounding a lagoon where the island used to be. The Lakshadweep and Maldives islands include atolls. Understanding the atoll (ring-shaped coral reef with a lagoon) is a prelims point. An atoll is a ring-shaped coral reef enclosing a lagoon, formed around a submerged volcanic island.

stem: A deep, steep-sided valley cut into the continental shelf and slope (resembling a canyon on land) is called a:
solution: A submarine canyon is a deep, steep-sided valley or gorge cut into the continental shelf and continental slope of the ocean floor — resembling a river canyon on land (but underwater). Submarine canyons are often found off the mouths of large rivers and are thought to be carved and kept clear largely by 'turbidity currents' (dense, sediment-laden underwater currents that flow down the slope). They are important pathways carrying sediment from the continents to the deep sea. Understanding the submarine canyon (deep undersea valley in the shelf/slope) is a prelims point. A submarine canyon is a deep, steep-sided valley cut into the continental shelf and slope.

stem: The Earth is often called the 'Blue Planet' because:
options: So much of its surface (about 71%) is covered by water (the blue oceans)
solution: The Earth is often called the 'Blue Planet' (or the 'Watery Planet') because such a large part of its surface — about 71% — is covered by water, mainly the vast oceans, which appear blue. When seen from space, the Earth appears predominantly blue because of this dominance of ocean water. This abundance of liquid water is unique to Earth among the planets of our solar system and is essential for life. Understanding why Earth is called the Blue Planet (dominated by ocean water) is a prelims point. Earth is called the Blue Planet because about 71% of its surface is covered by the blue oceans.

stem: The very cold ocean that surrounds Antarctica in the far south is the:
solution: The Southern Ocean (also called the Antarctic Ocean) is the ocean that surrounds the continent of Antarctica in the far south (around the South Pole). It is very cold, with much sea ice and icebergs, and it is encircled by the strong, unobstructed westerly winds and the powerful Antarctic Circumpolar Current that flows right around Antarctica. The Southern Ocean is one of the five recognised oceans of the world (Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, and Arctic). Understanding the Southern (Antarctic) Ocean is a prelims point. The Southern (Antarctic) Ocean is the cold ocean surrounding Antarctica.

stem: The smallest and shallowest ocean, located around the North Pole (largely covered by ice), is the:
solution: The Arctic Ocean is the smallest and shallowest of the world's oceans. It is located around the North Pole, in the Arctic region, and is largely covered by floating sea ice (pack ice), especially in winter. It is almost enclosed by the northern landmasses of Asia, Europe, and North America. (The world's five oceans, from largest to smallest, are: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, and Arctic.) The Arctic sea ice has been shrinking due to global warming. Understanding that the Arctic is the smallest, shallowest ocean (around the North Pole) is a prelims point. The Arctic Ocean is the smallest and shallowest ocean, around the North Pole, largely ice-covered.

stem: The lines drawn on a map joining places in the ocean that have equal salinity are called:
solution: Isohalines are the lines drawn on a map joining (connecting) places in the ocean that have equal salinity (the same saltiness). ('Iso' = equal; 'haline' relates to salt.) Isohaline maps are used to show the distribution of salinity across the oceans. (Compare: isotherms join places of equal temperature; isobars of equal pressure; isohyets of equal rainfall.) Understanding isohalines (lines of equal salinity) is a prelims point. Isohalines are lines joining places of equal ocean salinity.

stem: Water that is a mixture of freshwater and sea water — less salty than the sea but saltier than freshwater (as in estuaries, where rivers meet the sea) — is called:
solution: Brackish water is water that is a mixture of freshwater and salt (sea) water — it is more salty than freshwater but less salty than the open sea. Brackish water is typically found where rivers meet the sea (in estuaries and coastal lagoons and mangrove swamps), where the incoming freshwater mixes with the salt water. It supports special ecosystems (like mangroves) adapted to the intermediate salinity. Understanding brackish water (freshwater–seawater mix, intermediate salinity) is a prelims point. Brackish water is a mixture of fresh and sea water, of intermediate salinity, found where rivers meet the sea.

stem: The density of ocean water (its mass per unit volume) increases with:
options: Higher salinity and lower temperature (cold, salty water is densest)
solution: The density of ocean water increases with higher salinity and lower temperature — that is, cold, salty water is the densest, and warm, less-salty water is the least dense. Adding salt makes water heavier/denser, and cooling water also makes it denser (up to freezing). Because of this, the cold, salty, dense water tends to sink to the ocean depths, while the warm, lighter surface water floats on top; these density differences (driven by temperature and salinity — 'thermohaline' differences) drive the slow, deep circulation of the oceans. Understanding what makes ocean water dense (cold + salty) is a prelims point. Ocean-water density increases with higher salinity and lower temperature — cold, salty water is densest.

stem: The temperature of ocean-surface water at any place is influenced by latitude, the prevailing winds, ocean currents, and whether the sea is:
solution: The temperature of ocean-surface water at a place is influenced by several factors: latitude (surface water is warmer near the equator, colder toward the poles — the main control); the prevailing winds (winds blowing from the land or sea, and warm or cold winds, affect surface temperature); ocean currents (warm currents raise, and cold currents lower, the surface temperature of the areas they flow through); and whether the sea is enclosed (landlocked) or open — enclosed seas in low latitudes tend to have higher surface temperatures (e.g., the Red Sea) and those in high latitudes lower temperatures, because they are cut off from the open-ocean mixing. Understanding the factors controlling ocean-surface temperature is a prelims point. Ocean-surface temperature depends on latitude, prevailing winds, ocean currents, and whether the sea is enclosed or open.

stem: Warming and acidification of the oceans due to climate change can cause corals to expel their algae and turn white — a harmful phenomenon called coral:
solution: Coral bleaching is the phenomenon in which corals, under stress (mainly from unusually warm sea temperatures, and also from ocean acidification and pollution), expel the tiny algae (zooxanthellae) that live inside them and give them their colour and much of their food. Without these algae, the coral turns white ('bleached') and, if the stress continues, it starves and can die. Coral bleaching, driven largely by global warming (rising sea temperatures), is a serious threat to coral reefs worldwide (such as the Great Barrier Reef). Understanding coral bleaching (corals whitening/dying under warming stress) is a prelims-relevant point. Coral bleaching is the whitening (and death) of corals when they expel their algae under heat/acidification stress.

stem: The average depth of the oceans is roughly:
solution: The average depth of the world's oceans is roughly 3,800 metres (nearly 4 kilometres) — commonly cited as about 3,700–4,000 m. Although the oceans have shallow margins (the continental shelves) and some extremely deep trenches (over 11 km in the Mariana Trench), their average depth is close to 4 km, reflecting the vast deep-sea (abyssal) plains that make up most of the ocean floor. Understanding the approximate average ocean depth (~3.8 km) is a prelims point. The average depth of the oceans is about 3,800 metres (nearly 4 km).

stem: The depth of the ocean can be measured using an instrument that sends sound waves to the ocean floor and times their echo — a method called echo-sounding, using:
solution: The depth of the ocean (and the shape of the ocean floor) is measured using SONAR (Sound Navigation and Ranging), by the method of echo-sounding: an instrument on a ship sends a pulse of sound (sound waves) down toward the ocean floor, and measures the time the sound takes to travel down, bounce off the floor, and return as an echo; since the speed of sound in water is known, the depth can be calculated from this time. By taking many such soundings, oceanographers can map the relief of the ocean floor. (Radar uses radio waves and works in air/space, not for probing the deep ocean.) Understanding SONAR/echo-sounding for measuring ocean depth is a prelims point. Ocean depth is measured by echo-sounding using SONAR, which times the echo of sound waves from the ocean floor.

stem: Salinity is important for marine life and ocean processes; it also affects the __________ of sea water (and hence the movement of deep ocean currents).
solution: Salinity is important because, along with temperature, it affects the density of sea water (saltier water is denser/heavier). These density differences — caused by variations in salinity and temperature ('thermohaline' differences) — drive the slow, deep circulation of the oceans: dense (cold, salty) water sinks and flows along the ocean floor, while lighter water rises, setting up a global 'conveyor belt' of deep currents. Salinity also affects marine life (organisms are adapted to particular salinity ranges), the freezing point of the water, and evaporation. Understanding that salinity affects water density (and deep currents) is a prelims point. Salinity affects the density of sea water, which helps drive the deep ocean currents.

stem: The two arms of the Indian Ocean that border the Indian peninsula are the Arabian Sea (to the west) and the __________ (to the east).
solution: The two arms of the Indian Ocean that border the Indian peninsula are the Arabian Sea (to the west of India) and the Bay of Bengal (to the east of India). These, along with the Indian Ocean to the south, surround peninsular India on three sides. The Bay of Bengal (into which the Ganga, Brahmaputra, and many peninsular rivers drain) is prone to tropical cyclones, while the Arabian Sea lies to India's west (with important ports like Mumbai). Understanding that the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal border India is a basic prelims point. The Arabian Sea (west) and the Bay of Bengal (east) are the two arms of the Indian Ocean bordering India.

stem: Marine organisms that live on or in the ocean floor (the bottom) — such as crabs, starfish, and many shellfish — are called:
solution: Benthos refers to the marine organisms that live on, in, or near the ocean floor (the bottom) — such as crabs, starfish, sea anemones, worms, and shellfish (clams, oysters). The main groupings of marine life are: plankton (tiny organisms that drift/float with the currents — including phytoplankton, the plant plankton), nekton (animals that swim actively, like fish, whales, and squid), and benthos (bottom-dwellers). Understanding benthos (the sea-floor-dwelling organisms) is a prelims point. Benthos are the marine organisms that live on or in the ocean floor.

stem: The tiny, drifting/floating organisms of the ocean (including microscopic plants, phytoplankton) that form the base of the marine food chain are called:
solution: Plankton are the tiny, mostly microscopic organisms that drift or float passively in the ocean water, carried by the currents (they cannot swim against them). Plankton include phytoplankton (microscopic floating plants/algae) and zooplankton (tiny floating animals). Phytoplankton, through photosynthesis, form the base of the marine food chain (they are the 'grass of the sea' on which almost all other marine life ultimately depends) and produce a large share of the world's oxygen. Understanding plankton (the drifting organisms; base of the food chain) is a prelims point. Plankton are the tiny drifting organisms (including phytoplankton) that form the base of the marine food chain.

stem: Marine animals that can swim freely and actively in the ocean water (like fish, whales, and dolphins) are called:
solution: Nekton refers to the marine animals that can swim freely and actively through the ocean water, moving under their own power against the currents — such as fish, whales, dolphins, sharks, squid, and turtles. This distinguishes them from plankton (which merely drift with the currents) and benthos (which live on the sea floor). Understanding nekton (the free-swimming marine animals) is a prelims point. Nekton are the free-swimming marine animals, such as fish and whales.

stem: Enclosed seas in the hot subtropical latitudes (like the Red Sea) tend to have __________ salinity.
solution: Enclosed (landlocked or semi-enclosed) seas in the hot subtropical latitudes — like the Red Sea and the Mediterranean Sea — tend to have very high salinity. This is because they are in hot, dry regions with intense evaporation (which removes water and concentrates the salt), they receive little freshwater from rivers or rain, and, being enclosed, they have little exchange with the open ocean to dilute the salt. So the salt accumulates and the salinity rises well above the ocean average (the Red Sea, for example, is among the most saline open seas). Understanding why enclosed subtropical seas have high salinity is a prelims point. Enclosed seas in the hot subtropics, like the Red Sea, have very high salinity due to strong evaporation and little freshwater input.

stem: The oceans play a major role in the __________ cycle, as most of the water that evaporates to form clouds and rain comes from the ocean surface.
solution: The oceans play a major role in the water (hydrological) cycle, because most of the evaporation that supplies water vapour to the atmosphere (and hence forms clouds and precipitation) comes from the vast ocean surfaces. The Sun heats the ocean water, which evaporates into the air; this vapour condenses to form clouds and falls as rain and snow (over both sea and land); and the water eventually returns, via rivers and runoff, back to the oceans — completing the cycle. So the oceans are the great reservoir and source of the water cycle. (The oceans are also important in the carbon cycle, absorbing CO2, but their dominant role highlighted here is in the water cycle.) Understanding the oceans' role in the water cycle is a prelims point. The oceans are the main source of evaporation, so they play a major role in the water (hydrological) cycle.

stem: The oceans help to moderate the Earth's climate because water:
options: Heats and cools slowly (storing and releasing heat gradually), and ocean currents redistribute heat around the globe
solution: The oceans help to moderate (regulate) the Earth's climate because water heats up and cools down slowly — it has a great capacity to absorb, store, and release heat. So the oceans soak up heat when it is warm and release it when it is cool, moderating the temperature of the air above and of nearby lands (keeping coastal areas equable). In addition, ocean currents redistribute heat around the globe, carrying warm water from the tropics toward the poles and cold water back toward the tropics — which helps to even out the Earth's temperatures and prevents the tropics from overheating and the poles from getting ever colder. Thus the oceans act as a great regulator/moderator of world climate. Understanding the oceans' moderating role in climate (slow heat storage + currents) is a prelims point. The oceans moderate climate because water stores and releases heat slowly, and currents redistribute heat around the globe.

stem: The dissolving of extra carbon dioxide (from the atmosphere) into sea water, making the ocean water more acidic and harming corals and shellfish, is called ocean:
solution: Ocean acidification is the process in which the oceans absorb extra carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere (whose CO2 level has risen due to human activities); the dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, making the sea water more acidic (lowering its pH). This increasing acidity harms marine life that builds shells or skeletons of calcium carbonate — especially corals, shellfish (clams, oysters), and some plankton — because acidic water makes it harder for them to form and maintain their shells/skeletons. Ocean acidification, along with warming, is a major threat to coral reefs and marine ecosystems. Understanding ocean acidification (CO2 making the sea acidic, harming shell-builders) is a prelims-relevant point. Ocean acidification is the increasing acidity of sea water from absorbed CO2, which harms corals and shellfish.

stem: Which of the following correctly matches an ocean-floor feature with its description?
options: Continental shelf — the deepest part of the ocean
Ocean trench — the deepest part of the ocean floor
Abyssal plain — a steep slope near the coast
Mid-oceanic ridge — a shallow coastal area
solution: The correct match is: Ocean trench — the deepest part of the ocean floor. Checking the others: the continental shelf is the shallow (not deepest) submerged margin near the coast; the abyssal plain is the flat deep-sea floor (not a steep coastal slope — that is the continental slope); and the mid-oceanic ridge is an underwater mountain range in the deep ocean (not a shallow coastal area). Ocean trenches (like the Mariana Trench) are indeed the deepest features of the ocean floor. Understanding the correct descriptions of the ocean-floor features is a prelims point. Ocean trenches are the deepest parts of the ocean floor.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Water (Oceans)' is that:
options: The oceans are unimportant and lifeless

The oceans cover most of the Earth's surface and have a varied relief (shelf, slope, deep plains, ridges, trenches); their water has measurable properties like temperature and salinity that vary with place and depth; and the oceans are a vast, valuable resource vital to life, climate, and human use
The ocean floor is completely flat
solution: The chapter conveys that the oceans — which cover about 71% of the Earth's surface, making Earth the 'Blue Planet' — are a vast and vital part of the Earth. It shows that the ocean floor is not a featureless flat surface but has a varied relief, with major features including the continental shelf (the shallow, fisheries-rich submerged margin), the continental slope, the deep abyssal (deep-sea) plains, the mid-oceanic ridges (undersea mountain ranges), and the deep ocean trenches (the deepest points, like the Mariana Trench). It explains the measurable physical properties of ocean water — its temperature (which decreases from the equator to the poles and with depth, through the thermocline) and its salinity (averaging about 35 parts per thousand, but varying with evaporation and freshwater input). And it emphasises that the oceans are an immense and valuable resource — a source of food (fisheries), minerals, and energy, a medium of transport, a regulator of the world's climate and water cycle, and a home to abundant marine life — making them essential to life on Earth and to human society. Understanding the extent, the floor relief, the water properties (temperature and salinity), and the importance of the oceans is the central concern of this chapter. The oceans cover most of the Earth, have a varied floor relief and measurable water properties (temperature, salinity), and are a vast resource vital to life and climate.
